situation:
You are the channel manager for SUMMIT SPOKE TOURS, a guided bicycle touring company that has run multi-day rides through the river valleys for close to fifteen years. The owner (judge) built the business one route at a time and still approves every distribution decision personally. The owner (judge) has asked you to recommend how the company should sell its tour seats next season.

Summit Spoke Tours sells seats two ways: directly through its own website, and through roughly thirty independent bike shops that recommend the tours to their repair and rental customers in exchange for a referral commission. A written partner agreement promises those bike shops first access to new routes and prices no lower anywhere else. A new entrant, TRAILHEAD RIDES, sells nowhere but a large online travel marketplace and has been taking share for two seasons.

Last week an unexpected large order arrived. A national corporate travel agency will book four hundred seats for its client retreats next season, but only if Summit Spoke Tours lists its entire catalog on that same marketplace at the marketplace's fixed commission. Listing the entire catalog would break the promise of prices no lower anywhere else that the bike shops were given.

Taking the order means building a booking integration with the marketplace and hiring two reservation agents to staff it, an investment the company recovers only if the agency's four hundred seat forecast holds; if bookings come in lower, the integration and the two salaries are money already spent. Turning the order down keeps the bike shop agreement intact, but gives up the four hundred seats and leaves Trailhead Rides alone on the marketplace.

The owner (judge) wants you to analyze both channels, explain how you would identify the market the marketplace actually reaches, and recommend which channel strategy the company should carry into next season. The owner (judge) will greet you, hear your ideas, ask two questions, and thank you when the presentation and questions are over.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the owner of SUMMIT SPOKE TOURS. Business background is the same as the situation above. You built the routes yourself, you signed the partner agreement with the independent bike shops personally, and you have watched TRAILHEAD RIDES take share from the online travel marketplace for two seasons. The corporate travel agency's four hundred seat order is the largest single booking anyone has ever offered the company, and it comes with a condition you did not expect.

You have asked the channel manager (participant) to analyze both channels, explain how the company would identify the market the marketplace reaches, and recommend which channel strategy to carry into next season. You want to hear what the booking integration and the two reservation agents would cost if the forecast does not hold, and what happens to the bike shop relationships either way.

After the participant has presented, you will ask these two questions:
judgeQuestions: Who ends up paying for this decision if the four hundred seats do not sell?
Can we defend that outcome to the bike shops who signed our partner agreement?
